lessons.title: Lesson 59: Difficult words: 어쩌면, 아무래도, 가꾸다, 연세, 뵈다, 차림, 즉

grammar.explanation: 어쩌면 marks a guess the speaker isn't sure about, so it usually pairs with an ending like ~ㄹ/을지(도) 모르다 ('might'). In a question, it can instead express amazement, roughly 'how on earth is it that...?'.

examples.en: It might rain tomorrow.

examples.ko: 어쩌면 다음 주에 할아버지를 뵐 수 있을지도 몰라요.
examples.en: Maybe I'll be able to see Grandfather next week.
How did you manage to make the garden this pretty?

grammar.explanation: 아무래도 shows that the speaker, after weighing things up, thinks something is likely. It is usually paired with a guessing ending such as ~ㄹ/을 것 같다 or ~ㄴ/은 것 같다.

examples.en: It looks like I'll probably be late today.

examples.ko: 아무래도 그 사람이 벌써 떠난 것 같아요.
examples.en: He has probably already left.
It will probably rain.

grammar.explanation: 연세 is the respectful word for 나이 (age), used when talking about elderly people. 뵈다 is the humble/honorific version of 보다 for seeing or meeting someone you must respect; it conjugates like 되다 (뵈어요 → 봬요). 뵙다 means the same but is a bit more formal.

examples.en: How old is your grandmother?
I'm going to go see my teacher tomorrow.
See you next week.
Nice to meet you.

grammar.explanation: 가꾸다 means tending something carefully so it looks good. With plants, gardens or vegetables it means 'to grow/cultivate'; with 외모, 몸 or 머리 it means taking care of one's appearance.

examples.en: My father grows vegetables in the yard.
These days I'm getting in shape by exercising.
I need to fix myself up before the date.

grammar.explanation: 차림 refers to how someone is dressed. Put it after a clothing word (잠옷 차림, 운동복 차림) to say someone is in that outfit; 옷차림 is the general word for an outfit.

examples.en: My brother went outside in his pajamas.
He came to school in workout clothes.
Your outfit today is really nice.

grammar.explanation: 즉 introduces a restatement or clarification of what was just said, like 'i.e.' or 'in other words'. It often comes after a comma, before the rephrased part.

examples.ko: 그분은 제 아버지의 아버지, 즉 제 할아버지예요.
examples.en: He is my father's father, in other words my grandfather.

examples.ko: 시험은 다음 주 월요일, 즉 3일에 있어요.
examples.en: The exam is next Monday, that is, on the 3rd.

examples.ko: 그는 연락이 없어요. 즉 오지 않을 거예요.
examples.en: He hasn't been in touch. In other words, he won't come.

lessons.title: Lesson 60: Difficult words: 차다, 가득, 왠지, 설마, 찍다, 다행, ~달

vocab.en: to take (a photo); to stamp; to dip

grammar.explanation: 차다 says a space is filled; mark what fills it with (으)로. Although 찼어요 is past tense, it describes something full right now, and 차 있다 says the same thing as a state. The adverb 가득 adds the feeling of 'completely'. 차다 also works with feelings: Noun에 찬 = 'full of ...'.

examples.en: The bus is packed with people.
The bottle is full of water.
He spoke with a confident expression.

grammar.explanation: 왠지 comes from 왜 그런지 ('why it is so') and means 'for some reason' or 'I don't know why, but...'. Use it when something happens or is felt without a clear cause.

examples.en: For some reason I'm in a good mood today.

examples.ko: 왠지 그 사람이 마음에 안 들어요.
examples.en: I don't know why, but I don't like that person.
For some reason I want to go home early.

grammar.explanation: Putting 설마 at the start of a question shows the speaker can hardly believe something is (or isn't) the case, like 'Don't tell me...!' or 'Surely not...?'.

examples.en: Don't tell me you already ate it all?
Don't tell me you went alone?
Surely he didn't lie?

grammar.point: 찍다 (to touch one thing onto another)
grammar.explanation: 찍다's core idea is pressing or touching one thing onto another, so it covers taking photos, stamping a seal (도장), dipping food into sauce, and more. The object tells you which meaning is meant.

examples.en: My friend took a lot of pictures of me.
Please stamp your seal here.
I dip the dumplings in soy sauce and eat them.

grammar.explanation: Adding 다행이다 after a clause ending in ~아/어서 expresses relief that something happened or didn't happen ('Thank goodness...'). The adverb 다행히 means 'fortunately'.

examples.en: Thankfully the roads weren't jammed.
Thank goodness nobody got hurt.
Fortunately I wasn't late for the exam.

grammar.explanation: Adding 달 after a month name (3월 달) means 'sometime in that month' when the exact day isn't known or isn't important.

examples.en: I'm moving sometime in March.
My sister is getting married sometime in October.
I'm going to Korea sometime in May.

lessons.title: Lesson 61: To wish/to hope: 바라다, ~았/었으면 좋겠다

vocab.en: to swim, to move through water
to do all of, use up

grammar.explanation: 바라다 expresses wanting something to happen. To hope for a whole clause, nominalize the verb with ~기(를) and add 바라다. ~기 바랍니다 is also a formal, rather authoritative way of asking people to do something, often softened as ~아/어 주시기 바랍니다 in announcements. In speech, 바라요 is commonly pronounced 바래요.

examples.en: I hope everyone stays healthy.
I hope there will be a good result.
Please be quiet indoors.
I hope you have a good time.

grammar.explanation: Attach ~았/었으면 좋겠다 to a verb or adjective to say what you wish or hope for now; treat it as one fixed unit despite the past and future pieces inside it. ~(으)면 좋겠다 without the past tense is also used with almost the same meaning.

examples.en: I hope the weather is clear tomorrow.
I wish my friend would come pick me up.
I wish the exam would end quickly.
I wish I had a lot of money.

vocab.en: the first half of the year
the second half of the year
to build up, to stack up

grammar.explanation: ~(으)면서 joins two actions done at the same time by the same person: ~면서 after a vowel or ㄹ stem, ~으면서 after a consonant. It often translates as 'while' or 'as'. With 자라다 it gives 'grew up doing'. For posture verbs like 앉다 or 서다, use ~아/어서 instead, because ~(으)면서 would mean you were in the middle of sitting down.

examples.en: I study while listening to music.
I read the newspaper while drinking coffee.
I grew up eating Korean food.

grammar.explanation: With adjectives and 이다, ~(으)면서 says something has two qualities or roles at once. It is close to ~고, but feels like the two descriptions are tied together more closely.

examples.en: This restaurant is cheap and tasty at the same time.
He is a teacher and also a writer.
Today it's cloudy and cold.

grammar.explanation: ~(으)면서 can also connect two things one person does that clash, often when the speaker finds it unreasonable ('even though', 'yet'). Adding 도 (~(으)면서도) strengthens the contrast.

examples.ko: 그는 바쁘다고 하면서 하루 종일 텔레비전을 봐요.
examples.en: He says he's busy, yet he watches TV all day.
You know everything, so why are you asking?
She bought expensive clothes even though she has no money.

grammar.explanation: ~(으)며 is a shortened form of ~(으)면서 and can mean 'while', but ~(으)면서 is much more common for that. ~(으)며 is mostly used, especially in formal writing and speeches, to list or link related clauses, much like ~고.

examples.en: This city is clean and quiet.
The tourists laughed while taking pictures.

examples.ko: 상반기에는 판매가 늘었으며 하반기에도 늘 것입니다.
examples.en: Sales rose in the first half and will also rise in the second half.

vocab.en: to be made up of; to come true

grammar.explanation: Ending a sentence with ~ㄹ/을까 (without 요) can be a question the speaker asks themselves, such as 'Should I...?' or 'I wonder if...'. Context tells you whether it is self-talk or meant for someone else.

examples.en: What should I eat tonight?
Should I buy this book?
I wonder if it'll rain tomorrow.

grammar.explanation: When the speaker and listener will do something together, ~ㄹ/을까(요)? suggests it and asks for the listener's opinion: 'Shall we...?'. Add 요 for politeness. 그럴까요? is a common way to accept a suggestion.

examples.en: Shall we watch a movie together?
Where shall we meet?
Shall we take a short break?

grammar.explanation: When only the speaker will act, ~ㄹ/을까요? offers to do something and asks for permission, often right before helping or giving something. It pairs naturally with 드리다 or ~아/어 드리다.

examples.en: Shall I open the window?
Shall I help you?
Shall I get you a cup of coffee?

grammar.explanation: ~ㄹ/을게(요) is a statement, not a question: the speaker announces or promises what they will do, usually for or in consideration of the listener. It sounds softer and more cooperative than ~ㄹ/을 거예요.

examples.en: I'll open the door.
I'll call you again tomorrow.
I'll come right after I leave work.

grammar.explanation: ~ㄹ/을까(요)? can also ask the listener's opinion about how likely something is: 'Do you think...?'. Use ~았/었을까요? to guess about something that may already have happened.

examples.en: Do you think the weather will be nice tomorrow?
Do you think he's home now?
Do you think he already left work?

grammar.explanation: 어떻다 + ~ㄹ/을까요 becomes 어떨까요?, a gentle way to ask what someone thinks of an idea. ~는 게 어떨까요? politely suggests an action.

examples.en: How about this color?
How about going tomorrow?
What do you think about hiring more people?

grammar.explanation: Adding 하다 after ~ㄹ/을까 states a tentative plan: 'I'm thinking of / I intend to...'. It can be connected with ~아/어서 (~ㄹ/을까 해서) to mean 'I was thinking of..., so...'.

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 단풍 구경을 갈까 해요.
examples.en: I'm thinking of going to see the autumn leaves this weekend.
I'm thinking of going to bed early today.
I was thinking of going to the movies, so I called a friend.

grammar.explanation: At the end of a sentence, 보다 can replace 하다 with the same meaning of intent, almost always in the forms 봐 or 봐요. Don't use it mid-sentence with ~아/어서; use ~ㄹ/을까 해서 there instead.

examples.en: I think I might rest at home today.
I'm thinking of cutting my hair short.
I think I might have bibimbap for lunch.

grammar.explanation: Putting 하다 in the past (~ㄹ/을까 했다) shows that you had considered doing something but didn't actually do it. It is often followed by ~는데 or ~지만 and the reason.

examples.ko: 어제 친구를 만날까 했는데 비가 와서 못 만났어요.
examples.en: I was thinking of meeting a friend yesterday, but it rained so I couldn't.
I thought about taking a taxi, but I just walked.
I was thinking of changing my name, but I gave up on it.

lessons.title: Lesson 65: I am worried about: ㄹ/을까 봐

grammar.explanation: ~ㄹ/을까 봐 followed by 걱정되다 says you are worried something might happen. For something that may already have happened, use ~았/었을까 봐. 걱정되다 is often dropped, leaving just ~ㄹ/을까 봐(요), and context tells you it means worry rather than intent.

examples.en: I'm worried I'll fail the exam.
I'm worried the budget won't be enough.
I'm worried the child might have gotten lost.
I'm worried it might rain.

grammar.explanation: Follow ~ㄹ/을까 봐 with another clause to say what you did because of the worry. The tense goes on the final verb, not on the verb before ~ㄹ/을까 봐.

examples.en: I was worried I'd be late, so I took a taxi.
I brought an umbrella in case it rained.
I spoke quietly so the baby wouldn't wake up.

lessons.title: Lesson 66: Almost: 거의 and ~ㄹ/을 뻔 했다

grammar.explanation: 거의 is an adverb meaning 'almost'. It shows an action has nearly reached its end point (often with 다), or that something is very close to a description without quite matching it.

examples.en: I've almost finished my homework.
We're almost there.
These two bags are almost the same.

grammar.explanation: Attach ~ㄹ/을 뻔했다 to a verb for something that almost happened but never actually started, like nearly falling or nearly missing a bus. 뻔 is a bound noun with no meaning of its own, and since 'almost' is built in, 거의 is optional. It is almost always used in the past tense.

examples.en: I almost fell on the stairs.
I overslept and nearly missed my flight.
I saw a spider and almost screamed.
I very nearly hit the car.
